issues.explanation: "legally compulsory for every company worldwide" is unsupported. S01 (PDF page 4 / printed page 1) and S02 (PDF page 9 / printed page 6) state only that "the organization should quantify and report both totals" and that organizations "should calculate and report scope 2 emissions using two methods"; neither establishes a legal duty nor any worldwide applicability, and S01 is framed as guidance aligned with GHG Protocol for U.S. grid-delivered electricity.

The sources' recommendation modality "should" (S01: "The organization should quantify and report both totals"; S02: "Both results should be clearly labeled") is converted into "legally compulsory," i.e., a mandatory legal obligation, which the cited paragraphs do not express.

Facet f1 asks what the guidance recommends about reporting and labeling the two totals. The single claim omits the labeling recommendation in S02 ("Both results should be clearly labeled according to the method used") and misstates the reporting recommendation, so the requested facet is not answered.

The answer asserts a legal obligation applicable to "every company worldwide," which falls under the excluded areas of company legal applicability/compliance and outside the US-only jurisdiction scope; the evidence supports only conceptual explanation of EPA's recommendation.

The claim states a supplier's own generating stations "are enough to represent all electricity it delivers," which is contradicted by its own cited source. S12 (PDF page 10 / printed page 7) states the factor "must include all the electricity delivered by the supplier, including electricity it generates as well as electricity it purchases from others," and gives as an example of a factor that should NOT be used one that "only includes generation facilities owned by the supplier, which does not represent the full set of generation facilities supplying the delivered electricity." No cited paragraph supports the claim as written.

The facet asks what electricity a supplier-specific factor should represent. The only claim asserts the opposite of the source and never states the required content: the factor must cover all electricity delivered by the supplier, including both self-generated and purchased electricity (S12, PDF page 10 / printed page 7). The requested facet is therefore left unanswered.

S15 (PDF page 11 / printed page 8) states the opposite of the claim: where the agreement timeframe and reporting year do not align, "the emission factors for a purchasing agreement should only be applied to the portion of the reporting covered by that agreement," and a reporting year may be covered by two different agreements or partly uncovered. The wording "unusable in any part of an inventory year unless its start and end dates exactly match that year" is contradicted by, not supported by, the cited paragraph.

The facet asks how a mismatch between agreement dates and the inventory period affects the part of the period to which a factor can apply. The answer never states the material point from S15 that a non-aligned agreement's factor applies to the portion of the reporting year covered by that agreement (with full-year application only where timeframes align, and possible multiple or uncovered portions); instead it asserts total unusability, leaving the requested effect unaddressed.

"guarantees that its factor is eligible, without checking any other conditions" is contradicted by its own sources. S14 (PDF p.10) says "Refer to the quality criteria in Section 4 to ensure that an emission factor can be claimed based on the contract", and S13 says the same for certificates. No cited paragraph states bundling alone settles claimability.

Omits the source condition in S13 and S14 (PDF page 10 / printed page 7) that the Section 4 quality criteria must be consulted to ensure a factor can be claimed, and S14's condition that if certificates are sold to another entity the purchaser cannot make that claim.

S14 states the purchaser "can claim the emission factor"; the claim upgrades this permissive wording to "guarantees that its factor is eligible", asserting a certainty the cited paragraph does not express.

The facet asks what role quality conditions play in claimability, but the only claim denies any role and never conveys the cited requirement (S13, S14) to refer to the Section 4 quality criteria, nor the certificate-retention distinction in S14.

The answer issues a certificate/contract eligibility conclusion ("guarantees that its factor is eligible"), which falls under the excluded action "Contract/certificate eligibility decisions"; only conceptual explanation of conditions is permitted.

The wording "a supplier's renewable label alone does not establish certificate claimability" is not supported by its packet. S06 (PDF page 8 / printed page 5) only sets emission-factor boundaries (generation-only, no T&D or upstream), and S11 (PDF page 10 / printed page 7) only states that the market-based method considers contractual arrangements and that factor types are listed in order of preference. Neither paragraph mentions certificates, labels, or the conditions for claiming a certificate-based factor.

The claim's own citations (S06, S11) do not cover certificate claimability. The claimability conditions appear only in uncited paragraphs: S13 ("Refer to the quality criteria in Section 4 to ensure that an emission factor can be claimed based on the certificate", PDF page 10 / printed page 7) and S14 (certificates sold to another entity mean the purchaser cannot make that claim, PDF page 10 / printed page 7), which are outside this claim's citation dependency closure.

The claim states factor updates "always require every historic inventory to be recalculated with the newest edition." S16 (PDF page 12 / printed page 9) states the opposite: because periodic changes in emission factors do not represent a methodology change, "prior years' emissions need not be adjusted to reflect new factors." No cited paragraph (S16, S17, S18) supports mandatory recalculation of prior years for ordinary factor updates.

The claim omits the source condition that adjustment of prior years arises only in the methodology-change case: S17 (PDF page 12 / printed page 9) limits adjustment to changes in the methodology used to develop factors or a change in the type of factors used due to availability, and then only "in a manner consistent with the organization's base year adjustment policy."

"Always require" converts the sources' modality. S16 says prior years' emissions "need not be adjusted" and that use of the newest factors is "recommended"; S17 says prior years' emissions "should be adjusted" only for methodology changes. The absolute mandatory phrasing is not preserved from either cited paragraph.

Facet f1 asks how ordinary factor updates are distinguished from methodology changes for prior inventory years. The single claim asserts universal recalculation and therefore never states the distinction in S16/S17: routine factor updates do not trigger adjustment of prior years, whereas methodology changes (including a change in the type of factors used) call for adjustment consistent with the base year adjustment policy.
